Options A (18-month MPC lock-in), B (50% QIB) and D (Reg 30 disclosure) are all correct. Determinative point: UPSI does not wait for deal closure.

scenarios.scenarioText: Voltedge Power Ltd has a net profit (computed under Sec 198) of ₹40 crore and has no managing director or whole-time director. One of its directors, Mr. Ghosh, holds 25% of a counterparty with which Voltedge proposes a related-party contract. At the board meeting, Mr. Ghosh participated in the discussion and voted on the resolution approving that contract, and he had earlier failed to disclose his interest in Form MBP-1. Mr. Ghosh also absented himself from all meetings of the board held over a period of 13 months.

questions.question: Mr. Ghosh, interested in the related-party contract, participated in and voted on the board resolution approving it. Is this proper under Sec 184/188?

options.A: Yes — directors may always vote on contracts in which they are interested, provided they have disclosed the interest
options.B: No — an interested director must disclose his interest and must NOT participate in or vote on the resolution relating to that contract; his presence is also not counted towards the quorum for that item
options.C: Yes — voting is barred only for related-party transactions of listed companies
options.D: No — but only his vote is invalid; his participation in the discussion is permitted

questions.explanation: Sec 184(2) requires a director to disclose his interest and not to participate in the meeting's discussion or vote on a contract/arrangement in which he is interested; Sec 188 reinforces that an interested director cannot vote on a related-party transaction, and his presence is disregarded for the quorum on that item. Mr. Ghosh's participation and vote are therefore improper. Option A wrongly allows voting on disclosure; Option C limits it to listed companies; Option D wrongly permits participation in discussion. Determinative fact: Mr. Ghosh's interest plus his participation and vote.

questions.question: Mr. Ghosh failed to disclose his interest in Form MBP-1. What follows under Sec 184?

options.A: Nothing — MBP-1 disclosure is a mere formality with no consequence
options.B: Non-disclosure of interest is a contravention attracting a penalty under Sec 184, and a contract entered into without the required disclosure is voidable at the option of the company
options.C: He is automatically disqualified for five years
options.D: The contract becomes automatically void ab initio

questions.explanation: Failure to disclose interest in Form MBP-1 contravenes Sec 184(1)/(2) and attracts a penalty under Sec 184(4); further, under Sec 188(3)/general principles a contract entered into without the requisite disclosure/approval is VOIDABLE at the company's option. Option A treats it as inconsequential; Option C imports the Sec 164 disqualification; Option D says the contract is void (it is voidable, not void) — a precise but important distinction. Determinative fact: the MBP-1 non-disclosure.

questions.question: Mr. Ghosh absented himself from all meetings of the board held over a period of 13 months. What is the consequence under Sec 167?

options.A: Nothing — there is no minimum attendance requirement for directors
options.B: His office is deemed vacated — a director who absents himself from ALL meetings of the board held during a period of 12 months (with or without leave of absence) vacates office under Sec 167(1)(b)
options.C: His office is vacated only after 24 months of continuous absence
options.D: He vacates office only if he misses three consecutive meetings

questions.explanation: Sec 167(1)(b) provides that the office of a director becomes vacant if he absents himself from ALL the meetings of the board held during a period of 12 months, with or without leave of absence. Over 13 months Mr. Ghosh missed all meetings, so his office is vacated. Option A denies the rule; Option C uses 24 months; Option D applies a 'three consecutive meetings' test that is not the statutory standard. Determinative fact: absence from all board meetings over 13 months.

questions.question: Voltedge has no managing or whole-time director. What is the maximum remuneration payable to its non-executive directors (net profit ₹40 crore)?

options.A: 1% of net profits = ₹40 lakh
options.B: 3% of net profits = ₹1.2 crore — because the company has no managing or whole-time director, the cap for non-executive directors is 3% (instead of 1%)
options.C: 11% of net profits = ₹4.4 crore
options.D: 5% of net profits = ₹2 crore

questions.explanation: Under Sec 197(1), remuneration to directors who are neither managing nor whole-time directors is capped at 1% of net profits if there is a managing/whole-time director or manager, and 3% if there is none. Voltedge has no MD/WTD, so the 3% cap applies: 3% × ₹40 crore = ₹1.2 crore. Option A uses the 1% (with-MD) figure; Option C uses the 11% overall cap; Option D uses the 5% single-MD limit. Determinative facts: no MD/WTD + ₹40 crore net profit.

questions.question: Which statement about Voltedge is INCORRECT?

options.A: An interested director must not vote on the related-party resolution
options.B: Absence from all board meetings over a period of 12 months vacates a director's office
options.C: With no managing or whole-time director, the non-executive directors may be paid up to 1% of net profits
options.D: Non-disclosure of interest renders the contract voidable at the company's option

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. Where there is no MD/WTD, the non-executive directors' remuneration cap is 3% (not 1%), so Option C is false and is the answer. Options A (Sec 184/188 voting bar), B (Sec 167(1)(b) 12-month absence) and D (voidable contract) are all correct. Determinative point: 3% applies in the absence of an MD/WTD.

scenarios.scenarioText: Maharaja Industries Ltd, the listed flagship of the Maharaja Group, is under investigation by the SFIO for suspected fund diversion. While the investigation is on, a raider acquires 26% of Maharaja's voting rights. The company then enters CIRP under the IBC; immediately on admission, the moratorium takes effect, and an equipment lessor seeks to repossess machinery in Maharaja's possession. The liquidator later finds that the business had been carried on with intent to defraud creditors. A party aggrieved by the NCLT's CIRP order wishes to appeal.

questions.question: A raider acquired 26% of Maharaja's voting rights while the company was under SFIO investigation. Does the SFIO investigation affect the open-offer obligation under SAST?

options.A: Yes — an open offer cannot be made while a company is under SFIO investigation
options.B: No — crossing 25% triggers a mandatory open offer under SAST Reg 3 regardless of any pending SFIO investigation; the two regimes operate independently
options.C: No — but during an investigation the open-offer trigger rises to 30%
options.D: Yes — the open offer is suspended until the investigation concludes

questions.explanation: The SAST open-offer obligation is triggered the moment an acquirer crosses 25% of voting rights (Reg 3), independent of any SFIO investigation under the Companies Act; the two regimes operate in parallel. Option A and D wrongly suspend the open offer; Option C invents a raised 30% trigger during investigations. Determinative facts: 26% acquisition (crossing 25%) during the SFIO probe — integrating Ch 4 and SAST.

questions.question: During Maharaja's CIRP moratorium, the equipment lessor seeks to repossess machinery in the company's possession. Is this permitted?

options.A: Yes — a lessor's property rights override the moratorium
options.B: No — the Sec 14 moratorium bars the recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where that property is in the possession of the corporate debtor; the lessor cannot repossess during the moratorium
options.C: Yes — the moratorium applies only to financial creditors, not to lessors
options.D: No — but the lessor may repossess with the interim resolution professional's oral consent

questions.explanation: Sec 14(1)(d) of the IBC prohibits, during the moratorium, the recovery of any property by an owner or lessor where such property is occupied by or in the possession of the corporate debtor. The lessor therefore cannot repossess the machinery during the moratorium. Option A wrongly elevates the lessor's rights; Option C wrongly limits the moratorium to financial creditors; Option D invents an oral-consent exception. Determinative fact: leased machinery in the debtor's possession during the moratorium.

questions.question: When does the moratorium under the IBC take effect?

options.A: 30 days after the insolvency application is admitted
options.B: Simultaneously with the admission of the insolvency application by the NCLT, along with the appointment of the interim resolution professional
options.C: Only after the committee of creditors holds its first meeting
options.D: Only after a resolution plan has been approved

questions.explanation: Under Sec 13/14, the NCLT declares the moratorium SIMULTANEOUSLY with admission of the application (and appoints the IRP and causes a public announcement) — not after a delay or after the CoC/resolution stages. Option A introduces a 30-day delay; Options C and D defer the moratorium to later stages. Determinative point: moratorium is declared on admission.

questions.question: The liquidator finds that Maharaja's business was carried on with intent to defraud creditors. What is the consequence under Sec 339?

options.A: Nothing beyond the normal winding-up process
options.B: On the liquidator's application, the Tribunal may hold persons who were knowingly parties to carrying on the business with intent to defraud creditors PERSONALLY responsible, without any limitation of liability, for the company's debts
options.C: Only the company, as a separate legal entity, remains liable
options.D: Personal liability is capped at the amount of the director's remuneration

questions.explanation: Sec 339 (fraudulent conduct of business) empowers the Tribunal, on the application of the Official Liquidator/company liquidator, to declare persons who were knowingly parties to carrying on the business with intent to defraud creditors personally responsible, WITHOUT any limitation of liability, for all or any of the debts of the company. Option A ignores this; Option C clings to separate legal personality despite the statutory lifting of the veil; Option D invents a remuneration cap. Determinative fact: business carried on to defraud creditors.

questions.question: Which statement about the Maharaja Industries situation is INCORRECT?

options.A: Crossing 25% triggers a SAST open offer even during an SFIO investigation
options.B: The IBC moratorium bars a lessor from repossessing equipment in the debtor's possession
options.C: The IBC moratorium takes effect only 30 days after the application is admitted
options.D: Persons who carried on the business to defraud creditors can be made personally liable under Sec 339

questions.explanation: The question seeks the INCORRECT statement. The moratorium is declared SIMULTANEOUSLY with admission, not 30 days later, so Option C is false and is the answer. Options A (SAST trigger independent of SFIO probe), B (Sec 14 bar on lessor repossession) and D (Sec 339 personal liability) are all correct. Determinative point: simultaneity of the moratorium with admission.

scenarios.scenarioText: CONCEPT-BASED SET (no fact scenario): the following questions test integrated, cross-chapter mastery of numbers that recur across the Corporate & Economic Laws with DIFFERENT meanings. (Exam-sitting tags shown below are indicative of ICAI's recurring testing areas — drawn from memory-based recaps, RTPs/MTPs and past papers — and are not claims of verbatim reproduction.) Pick the option that keeps the colliding thresholds correctly apart.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · May 2023] Which statement correctly distinguishes the ₹1 lakh and ₹1 crore thresholds?

options.A: Both the Companies Act inability-to-pay demand and the IBC default threshold are ₹1 crore
options.B: The Companies Act statutory-demand (inability-to-pay) threshold is ₹1 lakh, whereas the IBC minimum default threshold is ₹1 crore (raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020)
options.C: The Companies Act threshold is ₹1 crore and the IBC threshold is ₹1 lakh
options.D: Both are ₹1 lakh

questions.explanation: Two different statutes, two different figures: the Companies Act inability-to-pay statutory demand uses ₹1 lakh, while the IBC minimum default for initiating CIRP is ₹1 crore (raised from ₹1 lakh by the March 2020 notification). Option C reverses them; Option A and D collapse them into one figure. The trap is that both were ₹1 lakh historically until the IBC figure was raised in 2020.

questions.question: Which statement about the '182-day' test is correct across the two laws that use it?

options.A: Both the FEMA residence test and the Companies Act resident-director test use 182 days measured over the calendar year
options.B: The FEMA 182-day residence test is measured over the preceding FINANCIAL year (April–March), whereas the Companies Act resident-director requirement (Sec 149(3)) of 182 days is measured over the CALENDAR year
options.C: FEMA uses the calendar year, and the Companies Act uses the financial year
options.D: Both use the financial year

questions.explanation: Same number, different windows: FEMA Sec 2(v) measures residence by presence of more than 182 days in the preceding FINANCIAL year (April–March), while Sec 149(3) of the Companies Act requires a resident director to have stayed in India for at least 182 days during the CALENDAR year. Option C reverses the two; Options A and D wrongly unify them. This is a classic cross-law collision.

questions.question: [ICAI-style · Nov 2023] Which statement correctly states the various super-majority/percentage thresholds?

options.A: An IBC resolution plan is approved by 75% of the CoC voting share
options.B: An IBC resolution plan needs 66% of the CoC voting share; a Sec 230 compromise needs three-fourths (75%) in value present and voting; a Sec 233 fast-track scheme needs members holding 90% of the total shares (by number); and a Sec 236 squeeze-out operates at 90% holding
options.C: All corporate-restructuring approvals require 90%
options.D: A Sec 230 compromise needs only a simple majority (over 50%) in value

questions.explanation: Each restructuring tool has its own threshold: IBC CoC plan approval = 66% (reduced from 75% in 2019); Sec 230 compromise = majority in number representing three-fourths (75%) in value present and voting; Sec 233 fast-track = members holding 90% of the total number of shares (and 9/10 in value of creditors); Sec 236 minority squeeze-out = 90% holding. Option A states the pre-2019 75% CoC figure; Option C over-generalises to 90%; Option D understates Sec 230. The trap is conflating these distinct percentages.

questions.question: Which statement about the '45-day' and '60-day' periods is correct?

options.A: The NCLT-to-NCLAT appeal period is 60 days and LODR quarterly results are due within 45 days
options.B: An appeal from the NCLT to the NCLAT must be filed within 45 days (condonable by a further 45, capped at 90); LODR quarterly results are due within 45 days and annual audited results within 60 days of the period-end
options.C: The NCLT-to-NCLAT appeal period is 90 days with no condonation
options.D: LODR annual results are due within 45 days and quarterly within 60 days

questions.explanation: Sec 421: NCLT-to-NCLAT appeal within 45 days, condonable by a further 45 (max 90). LODR Reg 33: quarterly results within 45 days of the quarter-end, annual audited results within 60 days of the financial year-end. Option A swaps the appeal period to 60 days; Option C drops the condonation and uses 90; Option D reverses the quarterly/annual periods. The trap is the recurring 45/60 swap.
questions.section: Companies Act Sec 421 / SEBI LODR Reg 33

questions.question: Which statement about the '5%/10%' disclosure and eligibility figures is correct?

options.A: PIT continual disclosure is triggered by a 2% change in holding
options.B: SAST requires disclosure on crossing 5% and on every 2% change thereafter; PIT continual disclosure is value-based (₹10 lakh in a calendar quarter), not percentage-based; and Sec 244 oppression eligibility (share-capital company) is 100 members or one-tenth of members, whichever LESS, or one-tenth of the issued capital
options.C: PIT and SAST use the same 5%/2% disclosure trigger
options.D: Sec 244 eligibility uses the HIGHER of 100 members or one-tenth of the members

questions.explanation: SAST Reg 29 uses a 5% acquisition disclosure and a 2% change-disclosure; PIT Reg 7(2) continual disclosure is value-based (traded value above ₹10 lakh in a calendar quarter), NOT a 5%/2% test; Sec 244 eligibility is 100 members or one-tenth of members, whichever LESS, or one-tenth of issued capital. Option A and C wrongly graft SAST's percentage triggers onto PIT; Option D uses 'higher' instead of 'whichever less' for Sec 244. The trap is the SAST↔PIT disclosure confusion.
questions.section: SEBI SAST Reg 29 / PIT Reg 7 / Companies Act Sec 244

scenarios.scenarioText: CONCEPT-BASED SET (no fact scenario): integrated questions on eligibility, waivers and forum/jurisdiction across the Companies Act. Choose the option that states the law correctly.

questions.question: Regarding waiver of eligibility thresholds, which statement is correct?

options.A: Both the Sec 244 and the Sec 245 thresholds can be waived by the Tribunal
options.B: The Tribunal may waive the eligibility threshold for a Sec 244 oppression petition, but there is NO power to waive the threshold for a Sec 245 class action
options.C: Neither threshold can ever be waived
options.D: Only the Central Government, not the Tribunal, may waive the Sec 244 threshold

questions.explanation: The proviso to Sec 244 expressly empowers the Tribunal to waive the eligibility requirement for an oppression/mismanagement application; Sec 245 (class action) contains NO such waiver. Option A wrongly extends waiver to Sec 245; Option C denies the Sec 244 waiver; Option D misattributes the power to the Central Government. The trap is assuming both provisions behave alike.

questions.question: Which statement about an SFIO investigation under Sec 212 is correct?

options.A: The SFIO shares jurisdiction with the State police and the CBI
options.B: Once assigned, the SFIO has exclusive jurisdiction; offences under Sec 212 are both cognizable AND non-bailable, and arrests may be made by authorised officers
options.C: SFIO offences are cognizable but bailable
options.D: The SFIO must hand the matter to the CBI for prosecution

questions.explanation: Once the SFIO is assigned an investigation, it has exclusive jurisdiction (no other agency may proceed), and the offences specified are both cognizable AND non-bailable, with a power of arrest for authorised officers. Option A wrongly posits concurrent jurisdiction; Option C makes them bailable; Option D diverts prosecution to the CBI. The trap is the 'cognizable but bailable' half-truth.

questions.question: Which statement about appeals and the bar on civil-court jurisdiction is correct?

options.A: A party aggrieved by an NCLT order may, as the first remedy, approach the High Court by writ
options.B: An appeal from the NCLT lies to the NCLAT; a further appeal to the Supreme Court lies only on a question of law; and civil courts are barred (Sec 430) from entertaining matters within the NCLT's jurisdiction
options.C: Appeals from the NCLAT to the Supreme Court lie on questions of fact
options.D: Civil courts have concurrent jurisdiction with the NCLT

questions.explanation: The statutory channel is NCLT → NCLAT → Supreme Court (the last only on a question of law under Sec 423), and Sec 430 bars civil courts from entertaining any matter which the NCLT/NCLAT is empowered to determine. Option A bypasses the NCLAT; Option C allows fact appeals to the Supreme Court; Option D asserts concurrent civil-court jurisdiction. The trap is forum confusion.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a trigger for a Central Government investigation into a company's affairs under Sec 210?

options.A: A special resolution passed by the company that its affairs ought to be investigated
options.B: An order of the Tribunal directing that the company's affairs be investigated
options.C: The Central Government forming an opinion (for instance, on a Registrar's or inspector's report) that an investigation is warranted
options.D: A written request by any single shareholder, irrespective of his holding, demanding an investigation

questions.explanation: The question seeks the option that is NOT a trigger. Sec 210 lists three triggers: (i) on receipt of a report of the Registrar/inspector; (ii) on intimation of a special resolution passed by the company that its affairs ought to be investigated; and (iii) in the public interest — and the Central Government MUST order an investigation when the Tribunal so directs. A demand by any single shareholder regardless of holding is NOT a statutory trigger, so Option D is the answer. Options A, B and C are valid triggers. The trap is forgetting that the company's own special resolution is a trigger while a lone shareholder's demand is not.

questions.question: Regarding privilege during an inspection/investigation under Sec 227, which statement is correct?

options.A: Neither a legal adviser nor a banker enjoys any privilege
options.B: A legal adviser's privilege is absolute and cannot be overridden, whereas a banker may be required to disclose a customer's information only if the Tribunal specifically so directs
options.C: A banker's privilege is absolute, while a legal adviser must always disclose
options.D: Both privileges can be overridden by the inspector acting alone

questions.explanation: Sec 227 preserves a legal adviser's privilege ABSOLUTELY, while a banker's confidentiality yields only where the Tribunal specifically directs disclosure of a customer's affairs. Option C reverses the two; Options A and D wrongly abolish privilege or let the inspector override it. The trap is treating the banker's and the legal adviser's positions as identical.

scenarios.scenarioText: CONCEPT-BASED SET (no fact scenario): integrated questions on statutory timelines and limits across the Companies Act, the IBC, SEBI SAST and FEMA. Choose the option that states the periods/limits correctly.

questions.question: Which set of meeting notice/gap periods is correct?

options.A: Board-meeting notice is 21 days and AGM notice is 7 days
options.B: A board meeting requires 7 days' notice, an AGM requires 21 clear days' notice, and the gap between two consecutive board meetings must not exceed 120 days
options.C: The maximum gap between two consecutive board meetings is 90 days
options.D: AGM notice is 14 days and board-meeting notice is 30 days

questions.explanation: Sec 173: board meetings require at least 7 days' notice and the gap between two consecutive meetings must not exceed 120 days; Sec 101: an AGM requires 21 clear days' notice. Option A swaps the two notice periods; Option C uses 90 days for the board-meeting gap (that figure relates to the minimum interval for OPC/small/dormant companies' half-yearly meetings); Option D uses wrong figures. The trap is the 7/21-day notice swap.

questions.question: Which IBC timeline is correct?

options.A: The NCLT must admit or reject a financial creditor's Sec 7 application within 30 days
options.B: The NCLT is to ascertain the default and admit/reject a Sec 7 application within 14 days; an operational creditor must serve a 21-day demand notice before filing; and CIRP must be completed within 330 days including any litigation
options.C: CIRP must be completed within 180 days, with no extension whatsoever
options.D: A financial creditor must serve a 21-day demand notice before filing under Sec 7

questions.explanation: Sec 7(4): the NCLT ascertains the default and admits/rejects within 14 days; Sec 8: an operational creditor must first serve a 21-day demand notice (a financial creditor need not); Sec 12: CIRP is to be completed within 180 days, extendable by 90 (270), and in any case within 330 days including time taken in legal proceedings. Option A uses 30 days; Option C denies any extension; Option D wrongly requires a demand notice from a financial creditor. The trap is the FC-vs-OC demand-notice distinction.

questions.question: Which SAST threshold is correct?

options.A: The open-offer trigger is 15% of voting rights and the minimum open-offer size is 20% of total shares
options.B: The open-offer trigger is 25% of voting rights and the minimum open-offer size is 26% of total shares
options.C: The trigger is 25% and the minimum open-offer size is 20%
options.D: The trigger is 26% and the minimum open-offer size is 25%

questions.explanation: Under SAST 2011, the substantial-acquisition open-offer trigger is 25% of voting rights (Reg 3) and the minimum open-offer size is 26% of the total shares (Reg 7). Option A states the pre-2011 (1997 Code) figures of 15%/20% — the amendment trap; Option C keeps the right trigger but the old 20% size; Option D reverses the two figures. The trap is the 15%/20% legacy numbers.

questions.question: Which FEMA limit is correct?

options.A: The Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) limit is USD 1,00,000 per person per financial year
options.B: The LRS limit is USD 2,50,000 per person per financial year, and export proceeds must be realised and repatriated within the period prescribed under Sec 7
options.C: The LRS limit is USD 5,00,000 per calendar year
options.D: There is no monetary limit under the LRS

questions.explanation: The LRS permits remittance of up to USD 2,50,000 per person per FINANCIAL year for permitted current/capital-account transactions, and FEMA Sec 7 requires export proceeds to be realised and repatriated within the prescribed period. Option A understates the LRS limit; Option C uses a wrong figure and the calendar year; Option D denies any limit. The trap is the USD figure and the financial-year basis.

questions.question: Which incorporation/first-meeting timeline is correct?

options.A: The first board meeting must be held within 90 days of incorporation
options.B: The first board meeting must be held within 30 days of the date of incorporation, and the first annual general meeting within 9 months of the close of the first financial year
options.C: The first AGM must be held within 6 months of incorporation
options.D: The first board meeting must be held within 7 days of incorporation

questions.explanation: Sec 173(1) requires the first board meeting within 30 days of the date of incorporation; Sec 96 requires the first AGM within 9 months of the close of the first financial year (and subsequent AGMs within 6 months of the close of the financial year, with a maximum 15-month gap). Option A uses 90 days; Option C confuses the 6-month rule (subsequent AGMs) and ties it to incorporation; Option D uses the 7-day notice period as if it were the holding deadline. The trap is mixing the first-AGM and subsequent-AGM rules.

scenarios.scenarioText: CONCEPT-BASED SET (no fact scenario): integrated questions on penalties and consequences across the SEBI Act, FEMA, the Companies Act and the PIT Regulations. Choose the option that states the consequence correctly.

questions.question: Which SEBI Act penalty is correctly stated?

options.A: The penalty for insider trading (Sec 15G) is a flat ₹25 crore
options.B: Sec 15G penalises insider trading at the HIGHER of ₹25 crore or three times the profit made, whereas failure to furnish information (Sec 15A) attracts ₹1 lakh per day, capped at ₹1 crore
options.C: Sec 15A penalises failure to furnish information at the higher of ₹25 crore or three times the profit
options.D: Both Sec 15G and Sec 15A cap the penalty at ₹1 crore

questions.explanation: Sec 15G (insider trading) and Sec 15H/15HA (takeover non-disclosure / fraudulent trade) impose a penalty of the HIGHER of ₹25 crore or three times the profit; Sec 15A (failure to furnish information/returns) imposes ₹1 lakh per day, capped at ₹1 crore. Option A drops the 3× limb of Sec 15G; Option C swaps the formulae; Option D wrongly caps Sec 15G at ₹1 crore. The trap is mixing the 15A cap with the 15G floor/multiple.

questions.question: Which FEMA penalty under Sec 13 is correctly stated?

options.A: For a quantifiable contravention, the penalty is a flat ₹2 lakh
options.B: For a quantifiable contravention, up to three times the sum involved; for a non-quantifiable contravention, up to ₹2 lakh; and a further ₹5,000 per day for a continuing contravention
options.C: For a non-quantifiable contravention, up to three times the sum involved
options.D: The continuing-contravention penalty is ₹1,000 per day

questions.explanation: FEMA Sec 13: where the amount is quantifiable, penalty up to three times the sum involved; where not quantifiable, up to ₹2 lakh; and where the contravention continues, a further penalty up to ₹5,000 for every day of continuance. Option A applies the non-quantifiable flat figure to a quantifiable contravention; Option C reverses the quantifiable/non-quantifiable treatment; Option D uses ₹1,000/day (a Companies Act-style figure). The trap is the quantifiable-vs-non-quantifiable swap.

questions.question: After the 2019 amendment, which statement about Sec 405 (failure to comply with a Central Government order to furnish statistics) is correct?

options.A: The default is punishable with imprisonment of up to six months and a fine of ₹25,000
options.B: It now attracts a civil penalty of ₹20,000, plus ₹1,000 per day of continuing failure, subject to a maximum of ₹3,00,000 — with no imprisonment
options.C: The penalty is the higher of ₹25 crore or three times any benefit obtained
options.D: There is no penalty for failing to furnish statistics

questions.explanation: Sec 405 was decriminalised by the 2019 amendment: the company and every officer in default are liable to a PENALTY of ₹20,000, with a further ₹1,000 per day of continuing failure, subject to a maximum of ₹3,00,000 — there is no imprisonment. Option A states the repealed criminal regime; Option C borrows the SEBI insider-trading formula; Option D denies any penalty. The trap is the pre-2019 ₹25,000-plus-imprisonment position.

questions.question: A designated person makes a profit on a prohibited contra-trade under the PIT Code of Conduct. What is the consequence?

options.A: A SEBI penalty of ₹25 crore
options.B: The profit is liable to be disgorged and remitted to SEBI for credit to the Investor Protection and Education Fund; this is a Code-of-Conduct consequence distinct from the Sec 15G penalty
options.C: The trade is automatically void and reversed by the depository
options.D: An automatic 10-year ban from the securities market

questions.explanation: Under Schedule B of the PIT Regulations, where a designated person executes a prohibited contra-trade (an opposite transaction within 6 months), the profits are liable to be DISGORGED and remitted to SEBI for credit to the Investor Protection and Education Fund — a Code-of-Conduct consequence administered by the company, distinct from the Sec 15G insider-trading penalty. Option A imports the ₹25 crore Sec 15G figure; Option C treats the trade as void; Option D invents an automatic ban. The trap is confusing disgorgement with the SEBI Act penalty.

questions.question: Which statement about punishment for fraud under Sec 447 is correct?

options.A: Fraud under Sec 447 is punishable only with a fine, never with imprisonment
options.B: Fraud under Sec 447 is punishable with imprisonment from 6 months to 10 years and a fine ranging from the amount involved to three times that amount; where the fraud involves public interest, the minimum imprisonment is 3 years
options.C: The maximum imprisonment under Sec 447 is 3 years
options.D: Section 447 applies only to listed companies

questions.explanation: Sec 447 punishes fraud with imprisonment for a term of not less than 6 months extending to 10 years, plus a fine not less than the amount involved and up to three times that amount; where the fraud involves public interest, the minimum term is 3 years. Option A denies imprisonment; Option C caps imprisonment at 3 years (that is the minimum in public-interest cases, not the maximum); Option D wrongly limits Sec 447 to listed companies. The trap is treating the 3-year public-interest minimum as the overall maximum.
